entity.name: John Adams
entity.description: The lawyer who defended British soldiers, then led American independence. John Adams risked his reputation to give the Boston Massacre soldiers a fair trial, co-drafted the Declaration of Independence, and became America's second president. He died on the Fourth of July, exactly 50 years after the Declaration was adopted — the same day as Thomas Jefferson.

story.name: John Adams
story.description: Defends the Boston Massacre soldiers, champions the Declaration of Independence, becomes the first VP and second president, and dies on the fiftieth Fourth of July.

moments.name: John Adams Is Born on a Farm in Braintree, Massachusetts
moments.subtitle: A deacon's son who will become the second president of a country that does not yet exist
moments.description: On October 30, 1735, John Adams was born on the family farm in Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts, to John Adams Sr., a deacon and farmer, and Susanna Boylston. The Adams family had been in Massachusetts since the 1630s. Young Adams attended local schools and entered Harvard College at age 16. After graduating in 1755, he briefly taught school in Worcester before deciding to pursue law. Adams would practice on this same farm for decades, and it remained his home base throughout his political career. His son John Quincy Adams, born nearby, would also become president — making them the first father-son presidential pair in American history.

moments.name: John Adams Defends the British Soldiers Accused of the Boston Massacre
moments.subtitle: The future revolutionary risks his career to ensure the king's soldiers get a fair trial
moments.description: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five civilians in what became known as the Boston Massacre. When no lawyer would defend the accused soldiers, John Adams took the case, believing every person deserved the right to counsel regardless of public outrage. The trial of Captain Thomas Preston began on October 24 and ended in acquittal. In December, Adams defended the remaining soldiers, winning acquittal for six and reduced charges for two. Adams made his famous argument that facts cannot be altered by passion or wishes. The defense demonstrated Adams's principled commitment to the rule of law — and remarkably did not damage his political career.

moments.name: John Adams Champions the Declaration of Independence in Congress
moments.subtitle: Jefferson writes it, but Adams is the one who fights for it on the floor
moments.description: In June-July 1776, John Adams served on the five-member committee appointed to draft the Declaration of Independence, alongside Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert Livingston. While Jefferson composed the text, Adams served as its primary advocate on the floor of the Continental Congress in Philadelphia. Adams argued passionately for independence, persuading hesitant delegates during heated debates. Jefferson later called Adams 'the pillar of its support on the floor of Congress, its ablest advocate and defender.' The Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776. Adams believed July 2 — the day Congress actually voted for independence — would be the great anniversary, but history chose the 4th.

moments.name: John Adams Becomes the First President to Live in the White House
moments.subtitle: The new executive mansion is so unfinished that Abigail hangs laundry in the East Room
moments.description: On November 1, 1800, President John Adams became the first occupant of the White House (then called the President's House) in the new federal capital of Washington, D.C. The building was far from complete — the plaster was still wet, there was not enough firewood, and only six of the roughly 30 rooms were habitable. When Abigail Adams arrived later that month, she famously used the unfinished East Room to hang laundry to dry. Adams lived in the White House for only four months before losing the 1800 election to Thomas Jefferson. He left Washington before dawn on Inauguration Day, becoming the first president to lose reelection — a bitter end to a distinguished career of public service.

moments.name: John Adams Dies on the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence
moments.subtitle: His last words reportedly reference Jefferson, who had died just hours earlier
moments.description: On July 4, 1826 — exactly 50 years after the adoption of the Declaration of Independence — John Adams died at his home in Quincy, Massachusetts, at age 90. According to tradition, his last words were 'Thomas Jefferson survives,' unaware that Jefferson had died at Monticello just hours earlier that same day. The extraordinary coincidence stunned the nation and was widely interpreted as a sign of divine providence. Adams and Jefferson had been political rivals who stopped speaking for years, but reconciled in 1812 and exchanged a remarkable correspondence of 158 letters in their final 14 years. Adams was the longest-lived president until Ronald Reagan surpassed his record in 2001.
